questions.passage: In 2019, archaeologist Elena Marquez used ground-penetrating radar to examine parts of Pompeii that had not been excavated. At the University of Naples Federico II, her team compared the radar images with maps of nearby Roman houses. The images revealed walls and courtyards beneath the surface, allowing the researchers to identify the layout of several buried structures without digging them up. The project showed that radar can help archaeologists study Pompeii while limiting physical disturbance to the site.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.A: Ground-penetrating radar can help archaeologists investigate Pompeii while reducing the need for excavation.
choices.B: Roman houses in Pompeii were generally larger than archaeologists had previously believed.
choices.C: Elena Marquez's team created the first complete map of Pompeii's buried structures.
choices.D: The University of Naples Federico II specializes in technologies for studying Roman architecture.

questions.explanation: The passage explains that Marquez's team used radar to identify buried structures without excavating them and concludes that the method can reduce physical disturbance. The other choices either focus on unsupported details or make claims the passage does not establish.

questions.passage: When archaeologist Elena Marquez and colleagues at the University of Naples Federico II surveyed an unexcavated section of Pompeii in 2019, they did not begin by removing soil. Instead, they used ground-penetrating radar and compared its readings with maps of nearby Roman houses. The resulting images suggested the presence of walls, courtyards, and other structural features below the surface. Because these features could be mapped without exposing them, the team could reconstruct portions of the area's layout while leaving the archaeological deposits largely undisturbed. The work therefore demonstrated that remote sensing can provide useful information about Pompeii while avoiding some of the physical disruption associated with conventional excavation.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.A: Maps of Roman houses are more useful than radar images for reconstructing Pompeii's buried structures.
choices.B: Ground-penetrating radar can reveal information about buried structures at Pompeii while allowing archaeologists to limit physical disturbance.
choices.C: Marquez's team's findings suggest that remote sensing can substantially reduce the need for conventional excavation at Pompeii.
choices.D: The structural features discovered by Elena Marquez's team were previously unknown to archaeologists.

questions.explanation: The passage connects the radar readings and existing maps to the team's ability to reconstruct buried structures without exposing them. Its central point is therefore that remote sensing can provide archaeological information while limiting physical disturbance. A and D misrepresent supporting details, while C extends the passage's claim beyond what it establishes.

questions.passage: At Pompeii, archaeologists seeking information about structures still hidden beneath volcanic deposits face a practical dilemma: excavation can reveal architectural details, but exposing deposits also physically alters the archaeological record. In 2019, Elena Marquez and colleagues at the University of Naples Federico II approached this problem differently. Their ground-penetrating-radar survey of an unexcavated area produced subsurface images that, when compared with maps of nearby Roman houses, indicated walls, courtyards, and other features beneath the ground. Such readings do not provide the same direct access to materials that excavation does, and individual signals can require interpretation. Nevertheless, the structural patterns visible across the radar images were sufficient for the team to reconstruct portions of the area's layout without first removing the overlying deposits. The significance of the project, then, lies less in showing that radar can replace excavation than in demonstrating that archaeological information about Pompeii can sometimes be obtained before excavation occurs. By making buried architecture accessible to study while leaving the deposits substantially intact, the method offers archaeologists a way to investigate the site while reducing the physical disruption that excavation can cause.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.A: Ground-penetrating radar provides archaeologists with more detailed information than conventional excavation does.
choices.B: Elena Marquez's survey established that the buried architecture of Pompeii can be completely reconstructed without excavation.
choices.C: Although radar cannot provide all the information that excavation can, it can reveal enough about buried structures to help archaeologists study Pompeii while limiting physical disturbance.
choices.D: The main purpose of comparing radar images with maps of Roman houses is to determine which areas of Pompeii should eventually be excavated.

questions.explanation: The passage establishes a tension between gaining information through excavation and preserving buried deposits. It then explains that Marquez's radar survey revealed structural patterns without exposing those deposits. At the same time, the passage explicitly limits the method's significance by noting that radar does not replace excavation or provide the same direct access to materials. C captures both the method's usefulness and its limitation. A reverses that limitation, B overstates the method's capabilities, and D describes a possible use of the survey rather than its central idea.

questions.passage: Since Eurasian beavers (*Castor fiber*) were reintroduced to Scotland, researchers have studied how their dams affect the movement of water. At Knapdale Forest, biologists observed that dams slowed water and temporarily stored some of it in ponds. During heavy rainfall, this storage delayed part of the runoff from reaching downstream channels all at once. As a result, water reached some downstream areas more gradually than it otherwise would have.
questions.question: Which inference is best supported by the passage?

choices.A: Beaver dams prevent heavy rainfall from entering Scottish streams.
choices.B: Knapdale Forest receives less rainfall than areas without beaver dams.
choices.C: Beaver dams permanently remove some stormwater from downstream channels.
choices.D: Beaver dams may reduce the intensity of some downstream flooding by delaying runoff.

questions.explanation: The passage explains that beaver dams slow water and temporarily store some runoff, causing it to reach downstream channels more gradually. It is therefore reasonable to infer that the dams may reduce the intensity of some downstream flooding. A, B, and C make claims that the passage does not support.

questions.passage: The return of Eurasian beavers (*Castor fiber*) to Scotland has given researchers an opportunity to examine how dam building affects water movement. At Knapdale Forest, monitoring showed that beaver structures could increase temporary water storage and delay the arrival of peak flows downstream. This effect would not make flooding impossible: stored water eventually leaves the ponds, and the amount of delay can vary with local conditions. Nevertheless, when runoff is slowed before reaching downstream channels, some of the water may arrive over a longer period rather than in a concentrated surge.
questions.question: Which inference is best supported by the passage?

choices.A: Beaver colonies may lessen the severity of some downstream floods by spreading the arrival of runoff over time.
choices.B: Beaver dams are most useful for preventing flooding when rainfall is relatively light.
choices.C: The presence of beavers guarantees that downstream flooding will remain minor.
choices.D: The Knapdale monitoring showed that beaver dams permanently retain stormwater.

questions.explanation: The passage states that beaver structures can temporarily store water and delay peak flows. Because some runoff may therefore reach downstream channels over a longer period instead of as a concentrated surge, it can be inferred that beaver colonies may lessen the severity of some floods. B, C, and D either add unsupported claims or contradict the passage's description of temporary storage.

questions.passage: The reintroduction of Eurasian beavers (*Castor fiber*) to Scotland has provided researchers with a way to examine how habitat modification can alter the timing of water movement. At Knapdale Forest, monitoring found that beaver structures could increase temporary storage and delay peak flows in some downstream streams. That observation does not mean that an individual dam can prevent flooding, since water stored in a pond eventually continues downstream and the amount of storage can change during a storm. The hydrological effect also depends on where dams occur within a drainage network. A structure located farther upstream, for example, can affect when part of its stored water reaches downstream channels, while a separate structure elsewhere in the same network can alter the timing of another portion of the runoff. Taken together, these observations indicate that the effect of beaver activity should be considered not only in terms of how much water a single pond can hold, but also in terms of how multiple temporary delays change the timing of runoff across a larger drainage system.
questions.question: Which inference is best supported by the passage?

choices.A: Because individual ponds eventually release stored water, beaver dams have little influence on downstream flood flows.
choices.B: Beaver dams can prevent major floods only when each pond remains below capacity throughout a storm.
choices.C: Several beaver dams distributed through a drainage network may moderate some downstream flooding by collectively delaying runoff, even though no individual dam guarantees flood prevention.
choices.D: The Knapdale study demonstrated that beaver structures are more effective than engineered flood-control systems.

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes between the limited effect of an individual dam and the combined effect of temporary delays at different points in a drainage network. Because multiple structures can alter when different portions of runoff reach downstream channels, their cumulative effect may moderate some downstream flooding even though none can guarantee that flooding will be prevented. A treats the eventual release of stored water as evidence that dams have little effect, ignoring the importance of delayed timing. B incorrectly assumes that permanent or uninterrupted storage is necessary. D introduces a comparison with engineered flood-control systems that the passage never makes.

questions.passage: Mangrove forests can reduce the force of coastal storms. In Florida’s Everglades, the red mangrove (*Rhizophora mangle*) forms dense networks of trunks and roots that slow moving water. Field measurements from the Ten Thousand Islands have shown that water loses energy as it passes through wider mangrove stands. However, a narrow or damaged stand provides less protection. Thus, mangroves can help shield coastlines from storm-driven water, especially when the forests are broad and intact.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.A: Broad, healthy mangrove forests can reduce the force of storm-driven water along coastlines.
choices.B: The red mangrove is the most common plant found throughout Florida’s Everglades.
choices.C: Researchers have found that storms are becoming more frequent in the Ten Thousand Islands.
choices.D: Mangrove roots are more important to coastal ecosystems than mangrove trunks are.

questions.explanation: The passage explains that mangroves can reduce the energy of storm-driven water and that broader, intact forests provide greater protection. The other choices focus on details that are either unsupported or not central to the passage.

questions.passage: Along Florida’s Ten Thousand Islands, stands of red mangrove (*Rhizophora mangle*) differ considerably in width and condition. Measurements of water moving through these forests indicate that the tangled trunks and aerial roots dissipate some of the energy carried by storm-driven water. The effect is not uniform, however: water passing through a narrow stand encounters fewer obstacles, while damaged vegetation likewise provides less resistance. These observations suggest that simply having mangroves along a shoreline does not guarantee the same degree of protection everywhere. Rather, the capacity of a mangrove forest to moderate storm impacts depends in part on how continuous and extensive the forest is.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.A: Red mangroves are especially well adapted to the environmental conditions of Florida’s Ten Thousand Islands.
choices.B: Mangrove forests can moderate storm-driven water, but the degree of protection depends partly on the forests’ extent and condition.
choices.C: Narrow mangrove stands are generally more vulnerable to storm damage than wide mangrove stands.
choices.D: The aerial roots of red mangroves dissipate more storm energy than their trunks do.

questions.explanation: The passage connects two ideas: mangrove vegetation dissipates some of the energy carried by storm-driven water, but the effect varies with the forest’s width and condition. Choice B combines both ideas into the central conclusion. A and D focus on narrower details, while C introduces a claim about vulnerability to damage that the passage does not establish.

questions.passage: In Florida’s Ten Thousand Islands, the red mangrove (*Rhizophora mangle*) occupies shorelines where storm-driven water can move inland with considerable force. Because the species develops substantial trunks and aerial roots, a mangrove stand does not merely mark the boundary between land and water; its vegetation also creates physical resistance to moving water. Measurements taken across stands of different widths indicate that this resistance can dissipate part of the water’s energy. Yet the presence of mangroves alone is an insufficient measure of their protective effect. A narrow stand may contain the same species as a much broader one but present far fewer obstacles to incoming water, and gaps caused by vegetation loss can similarly reduce resistance. Thus, two shorelines containing red mangroves may not receive the same degree of protection from storm-driven water. The distinction suggests that the ecological value of mangroves as a coastal buffer depends not simply on whether the vegetation is present, but on how much of the shoreline it occupies and how continuously it intercepts moving water.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.A: The protective value of red mangroves is determined primarily by the number of aerial roots in a coastal forest.
choices.B: Measurements from the Ten Thousand Islands demonstrate that storm-driven water causes extensive damage whenever mangrove forests are narrow.
choices.C: Red mangrove forests can lessen the energy of storm-driven water, although the amount of protection depends partly on how extensive and continuous the vegetation is.
choices.D: The presence of red mangroves along a shoreline is insufficient to prevent storms from carrying water inland.

questions.explanation: The passage first explains how red mangrove vegetation creates resistance to moving water, then qualifies that finding by showing that narrow or interrupted forests provide fewer obstacles. Its final point is therefore that mangroves can moderate storm-driven water, but their protective effect depends partly on the extent and continuity of the vegetation. A focuses too narrowly on aerial roots, B overstates the evidence, and D turns a qualification about the degree of protection into an absolute claim that mangroves cannot meaningfully limit inland water movement.

questions.passage: In ancient Pompeii, electoral messages called *programmata* were painted on walls along busy streets such as the Via dell'Abbondanza. These messages supported candidates for local office and sometimes named individual people or groups that endorsed them. Because political recommendations appeared in ordinary public spaces rather than only in official buildings, they provide evidence that political advocacy in Pompeii involved people outside the city's formal officeholders.
questions.question: What can reasonably be inferred from the passage about political advocacy in Pompeii?

choices.A: Most Pompeians supported the candidates named in public inscriptions.
choices.B: Political candidates were usually selected by wealthy patrons.
choices.C: Political advocacy in Pompeii was not limited to formal city officials.
choices.D: The Via dell'Abbondanza served as Pompeii's main political institution.

questions.explanation: The passage points out that electoral messages appeared in ordinary public spaces and sometimes identified people or groups endorsing candidates. These details support the inference that political advocacy extended beyond formal officeholders. The other choices make claims about the majority of Pompeians, candidate selection, or the importance of the street that the passage does not establish.

questions.passage: At Pompeii, electoral *programmata* appeared on walls along routes such as the Via dell'Abbondanza, where pedestrians could encounter recommendations for candidates seeking local office. Some inscriptions identify individual endorsers, while others refer to occupational or neighborhood groups. These messages cannot show how many Pompeians actually voted or how influential any particular endorsement was. They do show, however, that political advocacy was displayed in ordinary public spaces and could involve people and groups beyond those who held political office. The evidence therefore suggests that civic advocacy was connected to social relationships outside Pompeii's formal political institutions.
questions.question: Which inference is best supported by the passage?

choices.A: Political advocacy in Pompeii could extend through social networks beyond formal officeholders.
choices.B: Most occupational groups in Pompeii officially endorsed political candidates.
choices.C: The *programmata* were more influential than Pompeii's elections themselves.
choices.D: Neighborhood groups usually selected candidates for local office.

questions.explanation: The passage describes endorsements by individuals and groups and emphasizes that these messages appeared in ordinary public spaces. Although the inscriptions cannot establish the number of voters or the influence of particular endorsements, they support the inference that political advocacy extended through social relationships beyond formal officeholders. B, C, and D go beyond the evidence.

questions.passage: Pompeii's electoral inscriptions complicate the idea that local politics was conducted mainly within formal political spaces. Along streets such as the Via dell'Abbondanza, *programmata* recommended candidates for local office and sometimes identified individual endorsers or occupational and neighborhood groups. Their placement meant that political advocacy formed part of the visual environment encountered in everyday urban life. Yet the inscriptions reveal less about the scale of participation than about the existence of advocacy: they cannot establish how many people supported a candidate, whether an endorsement persuaded voters, or how many endorsers actually participated in an election. Even so, the range of people and groups represented in these messages suggests that political expression was connected to social relationships extending beyond officeholders themselves. The evidence therefore points to a political culture in which formal institutions existed alongside broader forms of publicly expressed civic advocacy, although the precise extent of that involvement remains uncertain.
questions.question: Which inference about Pompeii's political life is best supported by the passage?

choices.A: Because *programmata* were publicly visible, most Pompeians probably voted for the candidates they endorsed.
choices.B: Occupational and neighborhood groups held more political power than Pompeii's formal officeholders.
choices.C: The *programmata* demonstrate that Pompeii's elections were primarily controlled by ordinary pedestrians.
choices.D: Political advocacy in Pompeii likely extended through everyday social relationships, even though the scale of participation cannot be determined from the inscriptions.

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes between what the inscriptions demonstrate and what they cannot demonstrate. The variety of endorsers and the public placement of the *programmata* support the inference that political advocacy extended through everyday social relationships. However, the inscriptions do not reveal how many people actually participated or how influential the endorsements were. A, B, and C turn evidence of public advocacy into unsupported claims about majority behavior or political control.

questions.passage: At Pompeii, archaeologists have used ground-penetrating radar (GPR) to detect buried walls and other features beneath the site's surface. The scans can reveal patterns that may indicate structures that are difficult to see from above. Because researchers can survey an area before disturbing the ground, they can use the results to identify locations that deserve closer physical investigation. Thus, GPR can help archaeologists focus excavation on potentially informative areas.
questions.question: Which choice best supports the conclusion that GPR can help archaeologists use excavation more efficiently?

choices.A: GPR can reveal possible buried structures before archaeologists physically investigate the area.
choices.B: Pompeii contains structures from several periods of the city's history.
choices.C: Some buried features at Pompeii are difficult to detect from the surface.
choices.D: Archaeologists use several technologies when studying Pompeii.

questions.explanation: Choice A provides the direct link between GPR and more targeted excavation: researchers can identify possible structures before physically investigating them. The other choices provide relevant background but do not explain how GPR could make excavation more focused.

questions.passage: At Pompeii's House of Obellius Firmus, a georadar survey revealed several subsurface anomalies associated with buried wall structures. The results did not identify every feature with certainty; archaeological interpretation remained preliminary, and some locations required additional excavation to determine what the signals represented. Even so, the survey helped researchers distinguish areas containing potentially significant structural remains from portions of the site where fewer such anomalies were detected. Physical excavation could then be concentrated in places where the geophysical evidence suggested that further investigation might be especially informative. The radar therefore functioned less as a substitute for excavation than as a means of helping archaeologists decide where excavation could be most productive.
questions.question: Which choice best supports the conclusion that georadar helped archaeologists concentrate their excavation efforts?

choices.A: The survey revealed anomalies associated with buried wall structures, although their interpretation remained preliminary.
choices.B: Researchers used differences in the survey results to distinguish locations that warranted additional physical investigation.
choices.C: The House of Obellius Firmus contains buried structures that are not visible from the ground surface.
choices.D: Some features identified by the survey could not be interpreted with certainty without excavation.

questions.explanation: The conclusion concerns how georadar helped researchers concentrate excavation. Choice B connects the survey results to the researchers' decision about where to conduct additional physical investigation. A and D describe limitations of the survey, while C merely describes the archaeological setting.

questions.passage: At Pompeii's House of Obellius Firmus, archaeologists used georadar to investigate parts of the building whose earlier phases remained buried. The survey produced subsurface anomalies that were consistent with wall structures, but the signals did not by themselves reveal the complete form or history of those structures. Some interpretations remained tentative because different subsurface conditions could produce patterns requiring further investigation. This limitation might seem to reduce the value of the survey, especially when the archaeological questions concern construction phases or the arrangement of individual rooms. Yet excavation of selected areas produced physical remains that could be compared with the earlier radar interpretations. Where the two forms of evidence corresponded, the survey offered stronger grounds for treating particular anomalies as meaningful architectural features; where they did not, excavation supplied information that the georadar data had left unresolved. The contrasting results show that the usefulness of the survey cannot be measured simply by asking whether it independently identifies every buried structure. Its greater value emerges when the geophysical results are treated as preliminary evidence whose relationship to physical remains can determine where additional investigation is most informative.
questions.question: Which choice best explains how the evidence in the passage supports the author's conclusion about the role of georadar?

choices.A: Because georadar sometimes produces uncertain signals, excavation remains the more reliable method for reconstructing Pompeii's buried architecture.
choices.B: Because the survey identified anomalies that were later compared with physical remains, georadar can contribute useful preliminary evidence even when it cannot independently resolve every archaeological question.
choices.C: Because some radar anomalies corresponded to buried walls, georadar can determine the construction history of the House of Obellius Firmus before excavation begins.
choices.D: Because excavation can confirm or complicate radar interpretations, archaeologists should postpone georadar surveys until after physical remains have been uncovered.

questions.explanation: The passage develops a layered argument. First, georadar identifies potentially meaningful subsurface patterns, but those patterns are not definitive. Second, excavation supplies physical evidence against which the radar interpretations can be evaluated. Third, agreement between the two types of evidence strengthens the interpretation of some anomalies, while disagreement reveals where radar alone was insufficient. The overall conclusion is therefore that georadar is most useful as preliminary evidence that can help guide and inform further investigation, rather than as a complete substitute for excavation.

questions.passage: At the Red Mesa Research Station, engineers compared three photovoltaic arrays with the same rated capacity. The arrays received different amounts of sunlight and operated at different temperatures. Mesa received the most sunlight, at 7.4 hours per day, and produced the most electricity, at 20.1 kWh per day. However, Mesa also had the lowest efficiency, at 17.8%, while the cooler Juniper and Arroyo arrays had efficiencies of 19.2% and 19.5%, respectively.
questions.question: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage and table?

choices.A: Arroyo produced the most electricity because it had the highest efficiency.
choices.B: Higher temperatures caused all three arrays to produce more electricity.
choices.C: Mesa produced the most electricity even though it had the lowest efficiency.
choices.D: The three arrays received nearly identical amounts of sunlight.

questions.explanation: The table shows that Mesa had the highest daily electricity output but the lowest efficiency. The other choices contradict the data or make claims that the table does not establish.

table.caption: Photovoltaic array performance at Red Mesa Research Station

questions.passage: At the Red Mesa Research Station, engineers compared three photovoltaic arrays with the same rated capacity to examine how different operating conditions related to performance. Mesa received substantially more sunlight than Juniper or Arroyo and consequently had the highest daily electricity output. Yet Mesa also operated at the highest average temperature and had the lowest efficiency. The efficiency figures therefore cannot be interpreted simply by looking at total electricity production: an array may generate more electricity while converting a smaller percentage of the available sunlight. The data consequently distinguish between the amount of electricity an array produces and the proportion of incoming sunlight that it converts.
questions.question: Which choice provides the best evidence for the passage's distinction between total electricity production and conversion efficiency?

choices.A: Mesa operated at the highest average temperature.
choices.B: Mesa produced the most electricity while having the lowest efficiency of the three arrays.
choices.C: Juniper and Arroyo had lower daily electricity outputs than Mesa.
choices.D: All three arrays had the same rated capacity.

questions.explanation: B combines the two pieces of evidence needed for the distinction: Mesa led in total electricity output but had the lowest efficiency. The other choices provide only one part of the comparison or establish a condition under which the comparison was made.

table.caption: Photovoltaic array performance at Red Mesa Research Station

questions.passage: At the Red Mesa Research Station, engineers compared three photovoltaic arrays with the same rated capacity but different operating conditions. Mesa received 7.4 hours of sunlight per day, more than Juniper or Arroyo, and its 20.1 kWh daily output was likewise the highest. A simple ranking based on output would therefore place Mesa first. Yet the efficiency data complicate that ranking: Mesa converted 17.8% of the incoming sunlight, compared with 19.2% for Juniper and 19.5% for Arroyo, while also operating at the highest average temperature. The cooler arrays consequently converted a larger share of their available sunlight even though neither produced as much electricity overall. These results do not establish that temperature alone caused the efficiency differences, since the arrays were operating under different conditions, but the contrast prevents high output from being treated as evidence of superior conversion efficiency. At the same time, the lower efficiency cannot explain away Mesa's higher output, because Mesa received substantially more sunlight. The figures therefore leave two measurements pointing in different directions: one identifies Mesa as the daily-output leader, while the other shows that it converted a smaller fraction of the sunlight available to it.
questions.question: Which statement best synthesizes the information in the passage and table?

choices.A: Mesa's lower efficiency shows that increasing the amount of available sunlight does not substantially affect total electricity production.
choices.B: Because Juniper and Arroyo converted more sunlight efficiently, they should be considered superior to Mesa by every meaningful measure.
choices.C: Mesa's output advantage and efficiency disadvantage show that total electricity production and conversion efficiency measure different aspects of photovoltaic performance.
choices.D: The higher operating temperature at Mesa definitively caused its lower efficiency despite its greater exposure to sunlight.

questions.explanation: The passage creates an apparent tension: Mesa produced the most electricity but converted the smallest percentage of incoming sunlight. The student must recognize that these are different measurements, then use the table to resolve the tension rather than treating one measure as disproving the other. A incorrectly minimizes the importance of sunlight exposure, B turns one performance measure into an overall ranking, and D treats an observed temperature-efficiency pattern as proof of causation that the passage explicitly does not establish.

questions.passage: At the University of Arizona Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research, scientists study the annual growth rings of ponderosa pines in northern Arizona. In years with more rainfall, these trees often form wider rings. Because rainfall from centuries ago was not measured directly, researchers can use tree-ring width as a **proxy** for past precipitation. Thus, the rings provide an indirect way to estimate how wet earlier periods were.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“proxy”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: A feature that changes independently of environmental conditions
choices.B: A record that reveals exactly how much rain fell
choices.C: A method for predicting where trees will grow
choices.D: A substitute measure used to estimate something indirectly

questions.explanation: The passage explains that past rainfall was not measured directly, so researchers use tree-ring width to estimate it. Therefore, proxy refers to a substitute measure that provides indirect information about something else.

questions.passage: Researchers at the University of Arizona Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research have used ponderosa pine chronologies from northern Arizona to reconstruct rainfall patterns from periods before weather instruments were available. Wider rings often occur during wetter years, so ring width can serve as a **proxy** for precipitation. The relationship is not exact, however, because temperature, soil conditions, and other environmental factors can also affect growth. Researchers therefore compare many trees and calibrate their ring patterns against periods for which instrumental rainfall measurements are available. Once those influences are taken into account, variations in tree growth can provide evidence about rainfall that was never directly recorded.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“proxy”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: A collection of measurements used to distinguish one tree from another
choices.B: An indirect indicator used to estimate a quantity that was not directly observed
choices.C: A complete record that can replace instrumental measurements
choices.D: A biological characteristic that remains unchanged under different environmental conditions

questions.explanation: The passage explains that researchers use ring patterns to infer past rainfall even though the rainfall itself was not directly measured. Because the relationship must be calibrated and other influences considered, proxy means an indirect indicator, not an exact record.

questions.passage: At the University of Arizona Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research, scientists use ponderosa pine chronologies from northern Arizona to examine climate conditions that existed before systematic weather measurements. A wide ring may be associated with a wetter year, but the same measurement can also reflect temperature, soil moisture, competition, or other influences on growth. Researchers therefore do not treat an individual ring as a preserved record of the rainfall that produced it. Instead, they compare patterns across many trees and test those patterns against periods for which instrumental observations are available. A relationship that remains consistent after these comparisons can then be used when interpreting older portions of the chronology. This approach allows researchers to extract information about precipitation even though no rain gauge recorded the original conditions. For such reconstructions, the calibrated ring pattern functions as a **proxy** only because its relationship to precipitation has been established across independently measured periods.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“proxy”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: A measurement that becomes unreliable whenever more than one environmental factor affects it
choices.B: A direct record preserved from the period being studied
choices.C: A measurement used in place of a directly observed variable because a reliable relationship has been established between them
choices.D: A preliminary observation that must ultimately be discarded once instrumental records become available

questions.explanation: The passage does not treat ring width as a direct record of rainfall. Instead, researchers establish a relationship between ring patterns and instrumental precipitation data and then use that relationship to interpret earlier periods for which direct measurements do not exist. Thus, **proxy** refers to a measurement or indicator used in place of a directly observed variable because the relationship between them has been established.

questions.passage: Archaeologists studying pottery at the ancient settlement of Tel Haran first thought that the large number of painted bowls found there showed that the bowls had been made locally. However, chemical tests later showed that the clay came from a distant region, suggesting that many bowls had been imported. The researchers therefore described their first explanation as **provisional**, since the new evidence required them to reconsider it.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“provisional”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: Carefully documented
choices.B: Widely accepted
choices.C: Not yet final
choices.D: Based on chemical evidence

questions.explanation: The researchers had to reconsider their first explanation after receiving new evidence, so the explanation was provisional, or not yet final.

questions.passage: At Tel Haran, archaeologists initially connected the settlement's unusually large collection of painted bowls with local pottery production. The concentration seemed significant because nearby sites contained far fewer such vessels. Yet chemical analysis showed that the bowls' clay originated hundreds of kilometers away, making long-distance trade a plausible explanation. Some bowls also showed wear consistent with repeated use at Tel Haran, indicating that imported vessels could have accumulated there over time. For this reason, the researchers called their first explanation **provisional** rather than abandoning it entirely.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“provisional”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: Accepted as a reasonable possibility but still subject to reconsideration
choices.B: Supported primarily by evidence from nearby settlements
choices.C: Rejected because the pottery had been transported from elsewhere
choices.D: Established by the wear patterns found on the pottery

questions.explanation: The original explanation remained plausible, but the chemical and wear evidence prevented the researchers from treating it as settled. Thus, provisional means accepted for the time being but still open to reconsideration.

questions.passage: At Tel Haran, archaeologists initially connected the abundance of painted bowls with local production. The vessels were unusually common at the settlement, and fragments occurred in several areas where production debris might be expected. That interpretation remained **provisional**, however, because the distribution of fragments could also have resulted from the repeated use of pottery obtained elsewhere. Chemical analysis later linked the clay to a distant region, strengthening the case for long-distance trade but not establishing that every vessel had arrived that way. Some bowls showed extensive wear consistent with prolonged use at Tel Haran, whereas others were relatively little worn. The differing wear patterns therefore suggested that the collection might reflect several stages of acquisition and use rather than a single source. As a result, the chemical evidence weakened the original interpretation without eliminating it entirely; the researchers continued to treat local production as possible, but no longer as the only explanation for the settlement's unusually large pottery assemblage.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“provisional”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: Formed from evidence that was sufficient to establish one explanation conclusively
choices.B: Treated as a working interpretation even though further evidence could alter it
choices.C: Developed mainly by comparing Tel Haran with other archaeological settlements
choices.D: Restricted to pottery whose clay could be traced to distant regions

questions.passage: Researchers at Eastview University tested tomato plants in two urban farms. Plants watered with a drip system produced more tomatoes than plants watered by hand. The researchers noted that the drip system delivered water slowly, reducing the amount lost to evaporation during hot afternoons. Because the plants received water more efficiently, their **yield** was higher.

choices.A: Amount produced
choices.B: Amount watered
choices.C: Time required
choices.D: Temperature reached

questions.passage: At two urban farms, Eastview University researchers compared tomato plants watered by hand with plants using a drip system. The drip-watered plants produced more tomatoes, even though the researchers did not give them substantially more total water. This difference was especially noticeable on hot afternoons, when much of the water applied by hand evaporated before the plants could use it. Thus, the drip system's higher **yield** was associated with more effective delivery of water, although the researchers cautioned that the system did not increase the plants' total water supply.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“yield”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: Efficiency of water use
choices.B: Amount of tomatoes produced
choices.C: Total amount of water supplied
choices.D: Duration of afternoon heat

questions.passage: Eastview University researchers expected the tomato plants at two urban farms to respond mainly to the quantity of water supplied. The drip and hand-watered groups received nearly the same total amount over the study period, yet their **yield** measurements did not remain comparable. During hot afternoons, the hand-watered plots lost more water to evaporation, and the difference between the groups became especially pronounced. That pattern suggested that irrigation timing and delivery affected what portion of the supplied water was actually available to the plants, but the researchers did not assume that evaporation alone explained the result. When conditions were cooler and evaporation declined, the gap narrowed, although the drip-watered plants still maintained an overall production advantage. The researchers therefore interpreted the farm records by considering both the total water supplied and the conditions under which plants could use it. In this context, the relevant measure reflects the amount of agricultural output obtained under those conditions, rather than the volume of water applied.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“yield”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: The portion of water available to plants after irrigation
choices.B: The temperature conditions under which tomatoes grow
choices.C: The amount of agricultural output obtained from the plants
choices.D: The efficiency of the irrigation equipment itself

questions.explanation: The meaning of yield must be inferred by connecting the comparison of production, the discussion of water availability, and the final distinction between agricultural output and water applied. Yield refers to the amount of agricultural output obtained from the plants.

Chen therefore argues that a small amount of relevant background can help visitors understand historical objects.

questions.passage: At the Harbor City Museum, Mara Chen compared labels for nineteenth-century tools used by local shipbuilders. One version listed each object's name and date, while another added brief information about its use and connection to Harbor City's shipbuilding industry. Visitors who saw the second version more often identified the tools' functions correctly. However, Chen's longer experimental labels contained still more historical details, yet visitors did not consistently remember those additional facts. This result suggests that the value of a museum label may depend less on how much information it contains than on whether its information helps visitors interpret the object.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the primary purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that museums should replace historical information with simplified descriptions of objects
choices.B: To demonstrate that visitors to the Harbor City Museum prefer learning about local shipbuilding

choices.D: To compare the historical importance of the tools used by Harbor City shipbuilders with that of other nineteenth-century objects

questions.explanation: The text first presents the comparison of labels, then qualifies the result by noting that extra facts were not consistently remembered. The purpose is therefore to explain why relevant context can matter more than simply increasing the amount of information.

questions.passage: At the Harbor City Museum, Mara Chen investigated whether labels could help visitors understand nineteenth-century tools used by local shipbuilders. Her first comparison seemed to favor labels that supplied more information: visitors given names, dates, uses, and connections to the local industry encountered a fuller account than those given only names and dates. Yet visitors did not reliably retain the extra facts in the expanded labels, so the amount of information alone could not explain the results. A different comparison proved more revealing. Visitors who received shorter labels that included a tool's use and connection to Harbor's shipbuilding industry were more likely to identify its function than visitors who received only a name and date. The results therefore complicate a simple assumption that more historical detail should produce better understanding. They also suggest that the details most useful to a visitor may be those that establish a connection between an unfamiliar object and a larger historical setting, even when many other facts about the object are omitted.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the primary purpose of the text?

choices.A: To examine why the usefulness of museum-label information depends on how effectively selected details help visitors interpret an object's function and context
choices.B: To explain why providing historical information about museum objects can be counterproductive when visitors encounter too many details
choices.C: To show that visitors generally remember local historical information better than information about individual objects
choices.D: To trace how Mara Chen's research changed museum practices at the Harbor City Museum

questions.explanation: The passage first considers whether more information helps, then shows that visitors did not consistently retain the added facts, and finally contrasts those results with the stronger performance produced by concise contextual information. The purpose is to examine how the usefulness of label information depends on whether selected details help visitors interpret an object's function and historical context.

questions.passage: In the Netherlands, the Room for the River program gave some rivers more space to spread during high water by lowering floodplains and moving dikes farther from river channels. This approach can reduce flood risk without requiring rivers to remain permanently deeper or wider. During ordinary water levels, much of the added space remains dry, but during floods it temporarily holds excess water.

questions.passage: The Netherlands' Room for the River program changed several flood-prone areas by moving dikes, lowering floodplains, and creating additional channels. These changes allowed high water to spread over a larger area rather than forcing all of it through a narrow riverbed. Yet the added land was not intended to remain submerged: most of it functions as ordinary landscape until water levels rise. This distinction matters because the program's effectiveness depends not simply on creating more open water but on making space available when rivers carry unusually large volumes.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the purpose of the passage?

choices.A: To describe how permanent expansion of river channels protects Dutch cities
choices.B: To explain why moving dikes is generally less expensive than lowering floodplains
choices.C: To illustrate that the program's flood-control strategy relies on temporary use of additional space
choices.D: To suggest that flood-prone land in the Netherlands is unsuitable for ordinary landscape use

questions.explanation: The passage first describes how the projects create additional space and then clarifies that this space is normally dry. That distinction supports the broader purpose of explaining why temporary use of the added space is central to the flood-control strategy.

questions.passage:
When engineers evaluated projects in the Netherlands' Room for the River program, they initially focused on a simple result: after floodplains were lowered or dikes moved, peak water levels often fell. This pattern seemed consistent with the idea that enlarging a river's available space directly reduced flooding. Some sites complicated that interpretation, however. During ordinary flows, newly opened areas often remained dry, and vegetation sometimes covered them, making their contribution less apparent than that of a permanently widened channel.

Later high-water events revealed a different pattern. Those same areas were repeatedly inundated as rivers rose, although the timing varied with each site's elevation and shape. Sites with similar amounts of added area also produced different changes in water levels when their dikes and floodplains were arranged differently. Thus, neither the apparent inactivity of some restored areas during normal conditions nor the total amount of added land alone accounted for the program's results.
questions.question: Which choice best describes the purpose of the passage?

choices.A: To demonstrate that relocated dikes are more important than lowered floodplains in reducing flood risk
choices.B: To explain why restored floodplains are most effective when they remain covered by water for much of the year
choices.C: To compare the amount of land restored by different Room for the River projects
choices.D: To examine how observations under different water conditions challenge a simple explanation of why the projects reduce flood risk

questions.explanation: The passage begins with a straightforward explanation for the projects' effects, then introduces observations from normal and high-water conditions that complicate that explanation. The differing results among sites also show that the total amount of added land alone is insufficient. Together, these details support the purpose of examining why the projects' effects cannot be explained by a simple increase in available river space.

City planners often plant trees along sidewalks to reduce pedestrians' exposure to summer heat. In a Phoenix neighborhood, researchers found that shaded sidewalks were several degrees cooler than nearby unshaded pavement. The cooling was greatest where tree canopies directly covered areas used by pedestrians.

Text 2

A separate study of Phoenix streets found that adding trees did not produce the same amount of cooling everywhere. Trees that shaded sidewalks and other heavily used spaces provided the clearest reduction in people's heat exposure. Simply increasing the number of trees without considering their placement had a smaller effect.

choices.D: Cities should replace unshaded pavement with trees whenever possible.

questions.passage:
Text 1

In a Phoenix neighborhood, researchers compared sidewalks beneath mature tree canopies with nearby sidewalks exposed to direct sunlight. The shaded areas were cooler, suggesting that trees can reduce pedestrians' exposure to extreme heat. However, the researchers noted that the cooling benefit varied with canopy coverage: a street with many small trees did not necessarily provide as much shaded walking space as a street with fewer trees whose canopies were concentrated over sidewalks.

Text 2

Another study examined several Phoenix blocks after new trees were planted. Blocks with more trees generally became cooler, but the strongest reductions in pedestrian heat exposure occurred where the new trees were positioned beside frequently used walking routes. Some blocks gained substantial tree cover without a comparable reduction in the heat experienced by pedestrians.
questions.question: How does the second text relate to the finding in the first text?

choices.A: It challenges the first text's conclusion by showing that trees rarely reduce temperatures in urban areas.
choices.B: It extends the first text's finding by suggesting that the location of tree cover helps determine whether cooling reaches pedestrians.
choices.C: It provides an alternative explanation by arguing that the age of trees is more important than their placement.
choices.D: It narrows the first text's finding by showing that trees cool only sidewalks rather than other urban surfaces.

questions.explanation: Text 1 shows that canopy coverage affects how much shaded walking space trees provide, while Text 2 adds evidence that placement along heavily used routes influences whether that cooling reaches pedestrians.

questions.passage:
Text 1

In a Phoenix neighborhood, researchers found that sidewalks beneath mature tree canopies were cooler than nearby stretches exposed to direct sunlight. Because the difference was greatest during the hottest part of the day, the result initially appeared to support a broad expectation: increasing tree cover should make streets more protective during periods of extreme heat. Yet the researchers also observed stretches where several trees were present without creating continuous shade, leaving pedestrians exposed between canopies. This variation made it unclear whether the number of trees itself was the most useful measure of the benefit.

Text 2

A later study examined Phoenix blocks that received similar numbers of newly planted trees. Surface temperatures generally declined, but the change in conditions experienced by pedestrians varied considerably from block to block. Some blocks gained substantial vegetation while leaving long portions of commonly used walking routes exposed between separate canopies. Elsewhere, fewer trees produced a more continuous band of shade along routes with heavy pedestrian traffic. The researchers also found that blocks with comparable reductions in surface temperature could differ in how much relief pedestrians experienced during the hottest periods. These results made the relationship between vegetation and human heat exposure less straightforward than a simple tree-count comparison would suggest.
questions.question: The authors of the two texts would most likely agree that the second study

choices.A: demonstrates that reductions in surface temperature are less important than tree age when evaluating pedestrian heat exposure.
choices.B: suggests that the cooling observed in the first study should be understood partly in terms of where and how consistently tree cover reaches pedestrians.
choices.C: shows that increasing the number of trees has little effect unless every tree is planted directly beside a sidewalk.
choices.D: establishes that strategically placed trees can reduce pedestrian heat exposure even when they do not lower surface temperatures.

questions.explanation: Text 1 establishes that trees can cool pedestrian areas but raises uncertainty about whether tree count alone captures the benefit. Text 2 adds evidence that blocks with similar numbers of trees or similar surface-temperature reductions can produce different pedestrian experiences depending on how continuously the canopy reaches commonly used routes. Together, the texts suggest that the first study's cooling findings are most meaningfully interpreted in relation to the distribution and continuity of tree cover.

Researchers studying oyster-reef restoration in Maryland's Chesapeake Bay found that reefs can weaken incoming waves before they reach nearby shorelines. In test sites with restored reefs, shoreline sections behind the reefs generally lost less sediment than exposed sections. The researchers therefore suggested that oyster reefs can help protect vulnerable shorelines from erosion.

Text 2

A separate Chesapeake Bay restoration project produced similar results. Areas behind newly restored oyster reefs experienced smaller waves and retained more sediment than nearby areas without reefs. The project managers noted that the reefs were especially useful where wave action was contributing to shoreline erosion.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Researchers studying oyster-reef restoration in Maryland's Chesapeake Bay found that reefs reduced the force of waves reaching nearby shorelines. Shorelines behind restored reefs also retained more sediment than exposed shorelines. However, the researchers observed that the protective effect was strongest at sites where waves regularly approached the reef from the direction for which it had been positioned. Thus, reef restoration appeared useful for reducing erosion, but its effectiveness depended partly on local wave conditions.

Text 2

A Chesapeake Bay restoration project likewise found that restored oyster reefs could help stabilize nearby shorelines. Managers observed less sediment loss behind several reefs than in comparable unprotected areas. Yet reefs placed where wave directions frequently changed produced less consistent results. The managers concluded that restoration could contribute to erosion control when reef placement matched the conditions of the shoreline being protected.
questions.question: Which choice best describes how the second text relates to the first?

choices.A: It presents evidence that supports the first text's conclusion while adding that reef placement and local conditions affect the strength of the benefit.
choices.B: It challenges the first text by showing that oyster reefs generally fail to prevent sediment loss.
choices.C: It expands the first text's claim by arguing that oyster reefs protect shorelines regardless of changing wave conditions.
choices.D: It introduces an alternative explanation for erosion that the first text does not consider.

questions.explanation: Both texts find that oyster reefs can reduce shoreline erosion, but each also indicates that the benefit varies with local wave conditions and reef placement. Text 2 reinforces that qualification rather than replacing the first text's conclusion.

questions.passage:
Text 1

Researchers examining restored oyster reefs along Maryland's Chesapeake Bay initially found that shorelines behind reefs often retained more sediment than nearby unprotected shorelines. Because the reefs also reduced incoming wave energy, wave attenuation appeared to be a straightforward explanation for the difference. Measurements at several sites complicated that interpretation, however. Where currents carried sediment along the shoreline, a reef sometimes caused sediment to accumulate on one side while leaving another section more exposed. Later comparisons showed that reefs facing the dominant wave approach produced more consistent reductions in shoreline loss than reefs placed at other angles.

Text 2

A subsequent Chesapeake Bay project showed a similar pattern but introduced another complication. Instruments recorded weaker waves behind several reefs, and those areas generally lost less sediment. At one site, however, a reef reduced wave energy while erosion increased farther along the adjacent shoreline. Additional monitoring found that the structure had altered the path of a local current, shifting where sediment accumulated rather than simply preventing its movement. Other reefs, positioned differently relative to prevailing waves and shoreline currents, produced more stable shoreline conditions. Thus, sites with comparable reef structures and measurable wave reduction did not always show comparable patterns of sediment retention.
questions.question: Based on both texts, what is the most accurate conclusion about oyster-reef restoration in the Chesapeake Bay?

choices.A: Oyster reefs primarily protect shorelines by reducing wave energy, while changes in sediment movement have only a secondary effect on their performance.
choices.B: Oyster reefs can redistribute sediment without meaningfully reducing erosion, so wave measurements are an unreliable indicator of their value.
choices.C: The shoreline benefit of oyster reefs depends on how reef placement interacts with both incoming waves and local sediment movement, rather than on wave reduction alone.
choices.D: Because similar reefs can produce different sediment patterns, oyster-reef restoration cannot reliably contribute to shoreline erosion control.

questions.explanation: Text 1 first connects reef-related wave reduction with lower sediment loss, then shows that currents can redistribute sediment and that reef orientation affects the consistency of shoreline protection. Text 2 provides a parallel case in which wave energy was reduced but erosion increased elsewhere because a current's path was altered. Together, the texts support a more precise conclusion: reef performance depends on the interaction of placement, waves, and sediment movement, not on wave attenuation alone.

questions.passage:
A city archive is preparing a public exhibit about an 1890 map of the Riverside district. Curators initially valued the map because it shows streets and buildings that later disappeared, making it a useful record of the neighborhood's earlier appearance. A later city survey, however, places several property boundaries differently, and the surviving measurements in that survey appear more precise. This made it tempting to present the older map mainly as a historical image rather than as evidence that could be used to reconstruct Riverside.

Property records introduced a complication. Several parcels shown on the map were divided or recombined before the later survey was made, and the boundaries in the records changed again in subsequent decades. Aerial photographs later captured some of those same locations after additional changes had occurred. At the same time, several streets and buildings remained recognizable across the records. The exhibit therefore has to accommodate a record whose details do not always line up across dates, even though those differences occur within a neighborhood whose physical and property boundaries were themselves changing.
questions.question:
Which choice most effectively uses the information from the passage to accomplish this goal?

**Goal:** Explain why the 1890 map remains useful historical evidence without implying that its boundaries should match later records exactly.

choices.A: Although later records provide more precise information about some Riverside boundaries, the 1890 map remains useful because it documents streets and buildings from an earlier stage of the neighborhood's development.
choices.B: The 1890 map differs from later surveys because Riverside's property boundaries changed over time, so the map can help document those changes as well as the neighborhood's earlier appearance.
choices.C: Because several Riverside properties were divided or recombined after 1890, the later survey should be treated as more reliable than the older map when reconstructing the district.
choices.D: The 1890 map should be used alongside later surveys, property records, and aerial photographs, since differences among them may reflect both changes in Riverside and the limits of treating any single record as a complete account.

questions.explanation: The passage creates two competing interpretations: the later survey appears more precise, which could make the 1890 map seem mainly illustrative, but the property records and aerial photographs show that Riverside itself changed between the records. The best choice must therefore preserve the older map's value while acknowledging that discrepancies cannot be interpreted simply as errors. Choice D incorporates the map, later surveys, and records of change without treating any one source as a complete account.
